entries.title: How the Blackhawks plan to improve their defense without changing their systems
entries.summary: <p>After a team-wide reckoning Saturday night through Monday morning, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> elected not to overhaul their systems — or even make any major tweaks — but to instead bear down on numerous points of emphasis within those systems.</p><p>At practice Monday, they spent the first half working on defensive-zone coverage. Then they stopped for a rare mid-practice meeting before returning to the ice to work on tracking in transition.</p><p>Considering how inept the Hawks have looked at times this season — including throughout their 9-2 drubbing Saturday that prompted this reality check — fans may be confused why they wouldn't burn everything and start from scratch.</p><p>But coach Jeff Blashill, whose job security was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/08/blackhawks-jeff-blashill-no-coaching-changes-adjustments" >reiterated</a> by team sources Sunday, believes a rash decision like that wouldn't pay off Thursday against the Sabres.</p><p>"If you make full-scale changes to what you do, you could walk on the ice Thursday and guys [could] be super hesitant and not know what they’re doing," Blashill said. "And that’s the worst possible situation."</p><p>Blashill added players indicated "full belief in the systems" during team meetings Sunday. Everyone understands the Hawks need to allow fewer scoring chances than they have so far, though.</p><p>Natural Stat Trick's public model has the Hawks giving up the second-most chances (30.3) — per 60 minutes of five-on-five play — in the NHL. Blashill has been mocked plenty for the Hawks' internal stats, but they paint a comparable picture.</p><p>"Just [as] a big blanket statement, we've got to give up less chances," Blashill said. "The early part of the year, we didn't create much and we gave up a lot. As the year went along, we started creating more but we still gave up too many."</p><p>Blashill later said the Hawks have allowed the most two-on-one rushes in the league "by a lot," which certainly matches with the eye test.</p><p>Many of those rushes are enabled by players making mistakes within the Hawks' <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/16/blackhawks-forward-lineup-strategy-forechecking-puck-pressure" >aggressive 2-1-2 forecheck</a>, which Blashill admitted he would love to one day resemble the Hurricanes' renowned relentless approach.</p><p>Within that system, defensemen are encouraged to step up along the walls in the neutral zone, but the Hawks emphasized Monday they need to pick and choose when to do that instead of doing it automatically every time.</p><p>"On strong-side plays and on goalie-touch plays, [they need to] be way more cautious and aware of whether the 'F3' is there or not," Blashill said.</p><p>The F3s (high forwards) need to be more responsible, too. In particular, they need to stick to the middle of the ice instead of veering toward the wall. If they veer and the near defenseman steps up, that creates a situation primed for a two-on-one rush against.</p><p>"We want to be a pressure team, but you can’t chase pressure," Blashill said. "Sometimes you have to read those situations and live another day."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">An example of how not to forecheck from Saturday: Blackhawks have no F3 yet D Ian Cole steps up in the neutral zone anyway, leading to a 2-on-1 goal against <a href="https://t.co/q95ZZrD1ZF">pic.twitter.com/q95ZZrD1ZF</a></p>— Ben Pope’s Video Clips (@BenPopeCSTclips) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCSTclips/status/2119942836326125844?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 9, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Decision-making by defensemen within the defensive zone was another focus area Monday — in addition to basic defensive fundamentals like going "stick-on puck, body-on-body" and staying on the goal side of opponents.</p><p>The Hawks encourage defensemen to jump out from the net-front toward the boards if they can kill a play by doing so, but they need to rein in how often that happens.</p><p>"[The message was], 'Strike when you can in the 'D'-zone, but get to your post,'" defenseman Wyatt Kaiser said. "We [need to] be a little more cerebral, not just hanging on guys. Get to them, get back. If you can't get to them, let the center get to them. We don't need to be spreading out."</p><p>Blashill said the defensemen need to do "a better job of owning both posts," which involves "not getting tied up" with box-outs or going to the wrong post altogether.</p><p>It's worth noting the league's stoutest five-on-five defensive team (the Panthers) still allow 21.8 scoring chances per 60 minutes per Natural Stat Trick — only about 30% fewer than the Hawks do.</p><p>The margins are relatively slim in the NHL. That's why the Hawks believe a handful of fewer mistakes per game could actually make a big difference.</p><p>"Are you going to see a drastic difference next game? It's probably not going to look that different, to be honest," Kaiser said. "Maybe we win a few more battles, or [we] get a few blocked shots, or a few more shots come in and the 'D' are there and nothing happens.</p><p>"We're going to do what we do and do it a little bit better."</p>
entries.author: Ben Pope

entries.title: Blackhawks' problems start with GM Kyle Davidson
entries.summary: <p>Here’s the thing about rebuilds: They can keep people employed who shouldn’t be.</p><p>We’ve seen it from every team in town. Now we have the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" >Blackhawks,</a> who are in Year 5 of a rebuild that has gone off course.</p><p>After making strides last season, then raising expectations this season, the Hawks (4-13-1) entered Monday with the second-fewest points in the NHL — nine in 18 games. How bad is that? They’re on pace for 42 points, which would be their fewest in a full season since they totaled 31 in 1953-54, when a full season was 70 games.</p><p>So, yeah, things are bad, and it sure felt like the Hawks hit rock bottom Saturday night when the Stanley Cup champion Hurricanes pummeled them in a 9-2 game that wasn’t as close as the score indicates. That loss capped a horrendous 0-3 trip that had observers thinking significant changes could be coming. The Hawks were in crisis, and the coach’s seat appeared to be burning.</p><p>But when they practiced Monday, the general manager was not present.</p><p>Kyle Davidson began serving as interim GM in October 2021 after Stan Bowman resigned in the wake of the investigation into sexual-assault allegations against former video coach Brad Aldrich. The Hawks removed Davidson’s interim tag in March 2022 and have given him carte blanche to rebuild the team as he sees fit.</p><p>“There are some things that we need to fix that are going to take time,” Davidson said then. “Whether it’s three, five years, I don’t have an answer for that now. But we have to do this the right way.”</p><p>Well, three years came and went, and five years are now staring at Hawks fans, who are paying a tidy sum to watch bad hockey. So how does eight or 10 years sound? Because at this rate, the team won’t be rebuilt anytime soon, even with star center Connor Bedard around.</p><p>Davidson should’ve addressed all that and more Monday. Instead, he’ll speak to the media — and fans — Wednesday.</p><p>He’s in Toronto for GM meetings. His home is on fire, but he’ll put out the blaze in a couple of days. Would a Zoom call have killed him?</p><p>Coach Jeff Blashill was left to face the music again. Many thought his job was in peril — it still might be — but there he was Monday, leading practice and blowing the whistle to stop drills that had gone awry.</p><p>“Can’t have it!” he bellowed at one point.</p><p>Blashill, who coached mostly bad Red Wings teams from 2015 to 2022, is in a tough spot again. Like in Detroit, he doesn’t have everything he needs here, but he also isn’t getting enough from what he has.</p><p>He’s empathetic to the fans’ plight in all of this.</p><p>“I get the disappointment — our record is what our record is,” he said. “It’s not nearly where the fans thought it would be and not where we want it to be. We’re going to do everything we can to try to grind our way through this, get incrementally better, find our way to wins and, if we can do that, the satisfaction you get is awesome.</p><p>“That’s the only thing I could really say to [fans]. I can promise them whatever I want. That’s pretty much all bull---. We’re trying to grind like crazy to get better results through great process.”</p><p>The process that should be addressed is the one that procures players. Davidson went all in with the teardown, but he hasn’t done the same with the build-up. Yes, he acquired defenseman Bowen Byram and brought back Patrick Kane. But he didn’t do nearly enough to supplement all of his precious prospects with capable veterans. He could have addressed that Monday.</p><p>The biggest statement Davidson made in absentia was shipping out backup goalie Arvid Soderblom and calling up Drew Commesso. That’ll get the fans excited for the next home game Thursday, when the boo birds will fly at the first sight of folly. Davidson could’ve tried appealing to fans Monday, too.</p><p>And look who’s coming to town. It’s the Sabres, who went 14 years without a playoff berth before earning one last season. How many rebuilds is that? Do you remember the last time the Hawks went 14 seasons without making the playoffs? Of course you don’t, because it hasn’t happened — yet.</p><p>Davidson got lucky with Bedard as the No. 1 overall pick in 2023. Did he get unlucky or miscalculate by drafting Artyom Levshunov at No. 2 over Ivan Demidov in 2024? The jury is still out on Anton Frondell, the No.  3 pick in 2025. Meanwhile, other rebuilding teams are passing the Hawks left and right. Davidson could’ve talked about that, too.</p><p>Instead, we wait ’til Wednesday for Davidson to support the . . . let’s see . . . one, two, three . . . fourth coach he has hired.</p><p>When the popular perception is that the coach is the problem, it’s not a great look if the person who hired him isn’t there. If Davidson is spread too thin, maybe a director of hockey operations is necessary.</p><p>That way, someone would be there to put out the fire.</p>

entries.title: First day of practice: Is a new basketball powerhouse under construction at St. Laurence?
entries.summary: <p>St. Laurence’s campus has been under construction for a few years now, and a fieldhouse is going up next to the parking lot. That’s rare for a private school and a sign things are on the rise in Burbank.</p><p>If things go as planned on the basketball court this winter, St. Laurence might evolve from the most misspelled local high school into a new basketball powerhouse in the area.</p><p>Monday was the first day of practice across the state, and Roshawn Russell, who coached first-round NBA Draft pick Morez Johnson during his first three years at St. Rita, wore a wide smile as he discussed his current team. Russell is in his third year at St. Laurence and has one of the deepest, most talented squads in the state.</p><p>‘‘I love our group,’’ Russell said. ‘‘They have been together for a while and are very close. Ups and downs are expected, but they will be able to handle any adversity. This may be the deepest team I’ve had, one through 15. I’m confident in putting anyone in the game.’’</p><p>Senior Markese Peoples, a 6-2 guard who recently switched his college commitment from Central Michigan to UIC, is one of only six Division I seniors in the area.</p><p>‘‘Markese is unguardable,’’ Russell said. “He’s a leader and a great person, and his teammates love him. We will go as he goes. He knows that. He is the senior that will be on the floor the most, and we will follow his lead.’’</p><p>Peoples is rugged and physical, able to bully his way into the paint to score and rebound. He averaged 17 points and seven rebounds last season, but he took his game to a new level during the summer.</p><p>‘‘I’m stronger than most guards but able to do guard things,’’ Peoples said. ‘‘It is fun battling down low.’’</p><p>Peoples went under the radar last season but is considered one of the top players in the area and had his choice of several colleges.</p><p>‘‘Everything fell into place in a short period of time,’’ he said. “I love everything around [St. Laurence]. It changed my life, really. I’m forever thankful for what St. Laurence gave me.’’</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-250000" name="image-250000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6ce06da/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5388x3024+0+284/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2Fb0%2F13ba2af5442f93742f60c4e6e746%2Fob-cst-111026-006.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d82ea0c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5388x3024+0+284/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2Fb0%2F13ba2af5442f93742f60c4e6e746%2Fob-cst-111026-006.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1ca461d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5388x3024+0+284/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2Fb0%2F13ba2af5442f93742f60c4e6e746%2Fob-cst-111026-006.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="St. Laurence coach Roshawn Russell coaches Noah Corro (5), Markese Peoples (23) and Jeremiah Toney (4) on the first day of basketball practice. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1ca461d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5388x3024+0+284/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2Fb0%2F13ba2af5442f93742f60c4e6e746%2Fob-cst-111026-006.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/68e60f2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5388x3024+0+284/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2Fb0%2F13ba2af5442f93742f60c4e6e746%2Fob-cst-111026-006.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1ca461d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5388x3024+0+284/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2Fb0%2F13ba2af5442f93742f60c4e6e746%2Fob-cst-111026-006.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>St. Laurence coach Roshawn Russell coaches Noah Corro (5), Markese Peoples (23) and Jeremiah Toney (4) on the first day of basketball practice.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kirsten Stickney/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Three experienced juniors also return: 6-6 Logan Brown, 6-4 Jeremiah Toney and 6-2 Noah Corro. Sophomores Evan Lemons and Lawrence Burnett will be major contributors, and Russell also expects 6-5 freshman Bennett Meier and 6-0 freshman Dakarai Simmons to pitch in.</p><p>‘‘Logan is a lot stronger, and his confidence level has risen,’’ Russell said. ‘‘He’s been a three-sport athlete all his life, Now he’s locked in on basketball, and the hard work is paying off.’’</p><p>Lemons is long and athletic and might be one of the breakout sophomores in the state.</p><p>The Vikings will need substantial contributions from the young stars because their schedule is extremely challenging. They open the season at the prestigious Tournament of Champions in Washington, play in all the top local events and will travel to Las Vegas for the Tarkanian Classic.</p><p>‘‘Nowadays, it is really difficult for a high-school kid to get college opportunities,’’ Russell said. ‘‘We have big goals and want to accomplish a lot this year, but my No. 1 will always be helping kids get to college. We have to play in some very competitive tournaments for these guys to be seen.’’</p><p>If Peoples lives up to his promise this winter and the young players around him continue to mature, anything is possible for St. Laurence.</p><p>‘‘I am hearing about the basketball team every day,’’ Toney said. ‘‘The school is definitely excited about the season.’’</p>

entries.title: Bridgeport neighbors raise concerns about police driving and scooter traffic after fatal crash
entries.summary: <p>A 39-year-old man riding a stand-up electric scooter was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/05/electric-scooter-driver-dead-after-collision-with-cpd-vehicle-in-bridgeport" target="_blank" >killed last Thursday</a> after colliding with a marked Chicago police vehicle in Bridgeport, prompting nearby residents to raise concerns about driving habits and traffic safety in the neighborhood.</p><p>The victim, identified Monday as Bridgeport resident Hao Lin by the Cook County Medical Examiner’s Office, lived in the 3200 block of South Wallace Street. He was pronounced dead at 1:15 a.m. at Stroger Hospital , according to Chicago police.</p><p>According to Chicago police, officers were northbound on Princeton Avenue in a marked police vehicle while on patrol when their vehicle collided with the electric scooter operated by Lin.</p><p>Lin was treated at the scene by Chicago Fire Department personnel before being transported to Stroger, police said. The results of Lin's autopsy remain inconclusive, according to the medical examiner's office.</p><p>Both officers inside the police vehicle were transported to University of Illinois Hospital for treatment.</p><p>The circumstances surrounding the crash remain under investigation by CPD's Major Accidents Investigation Unit, so it's not yet known whether the officers or Lin are at fault. And Bridgeport residents interviewed said they see both police and scooter riders driving unsafely in the area.</p><p>Sira Rivera, a Bridgeport resident of more than five years who lives less than four blocks from the crash scene. He didn't see the crash but said he wasn't completely surprised it involved a police vehicle.</p><p>“The cops always run the stop signs in the neighborhood,” Rivera said. “They drive kind of crazy all the time.”</p><p>Other residents pointed to dangerous behavior among electric scooter and bicycle riders, saying they frequently ignore stop signs and traffic signals, creating risks for themselves and others.</p><p>Frank, a lifelong Bridgeport resident who declined to provide his last name, lives about a block from the crash scene. He said he’s noticed a pattern of scooter and bicycle riders disregarding traffic signals.</p><p>“A lot of scooter people just run right through the stop signs, the stoplights,” he said. </p><p>Concerns about scooter safety in Chicago come amid <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/06/electric-scooter-driver-67-killed-in-c" target="_blank" >another fatal crash involving an electric scooter last week.</a> The day after Lin's death, a 67-year-old man riding a stand-up electric scooter was killed in North Park after being struck by a speeding SUV.</p><p>Frank said riders who fail to stop at intersections put themselves at risk, particularly when vehicles approach at higher speeds.</p><p>He said scooter and bicycle riders should follow the same traffic rules as motorists.</p><p></p><p>“If everyone just sits there and abides by the laws of stopping at the stop signs or stoplights, I think it will go down a whole lot,” he added.</p>
entries.author: Christiana Freitag

entries.title: Mayor Johnson upends gunshot-detection pilot after voters resoundingly back the technology
entries.summary: <p>The 72% support in an advisory referendum for bringing gunshot-detection technology back to the streets of Chicago has apparently prompted Mayor Brandon Johnson to change his crime-fighting strategy.</p><p>Chief Procurement Officer Sharla Roberts disclosed the surprise about-face Monday while on the hot seat at a City Council budget hearing.</p><p>Roberts said her office initially planned a pilot program with one vendor that wasn't involved in a lengthy, competitive bidding process for a gunshot-detection contract. But the Johnson administration has now decided to let all of the “short-listed” bidders showcase their violence prevention strategies in the pilot, Roberts said.</p><p>The mystery program will still test a variety of ideas, including more violence intervention, “drone-based situational awareness, license plate recognition and incident response systems for evidence preservation.”</p><p>Gunshot-detection technology is still only part of the pilot.</p><p>Roberts acknowledged <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/04/shotspotter-advisory-referendum-gunshot-detection-technology-brandon-johnson-opposition" >voters’ support</a> for a technology her boss had scrapped prompted the administration to change course.</p><p>“The information from the referendum does play [into the mayor’s thinking] because … it spoke loudly. That’s what the community wants. So we are listening — not just to the alders. We’re listening to what the community wanted just as well,” Roberts said.</p><p>Input from police district personnel and a veiled warning from SoundThinking, the parent company of ShotSpotter, also contributed to Johnson's shift, Roberts said. The mayor got rid of ShotSpotter in 2024.</p><p>In an Oct. 27 letter, SoundThinking's attorney informed Roberts that, if the city was, in fact, planning to test crime-fighting strategies that included gunshot detection, ShotSpotter demanded to be part of it because the company was one of the “short-listed” firms.</p><p>A SoundThinking spokesperson said Johnson’s administration never contacted the company after its fall 2025 oral presentation and live-fire demonstration with the city. The spokesperson said the voters who backed the recent referendum on gunshot-detection technology "deserve to be heard, particularly in communities where gun violence is, unfortunately, a lived experience."</p><p>Far South Side Ald. Anthony Beale (9th), one of Johnson’s most outspoken Council critics, has accused the mayor of using the pilot as a stalling tactic to get past the mayoral election.</p><p>Beale likened the mayor’s change in strategy to playing Russian roulette with the lives of everyday Chicagoans.</p><p>“People are bleeding out in the street every single day because we don't have this technology, and we don't have time to play games with a hypothetical pilot program that we're making up in order to make it seem like we're doing something,” Beale told Roberts.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> about-face on gunshot detection technology.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>LinkedIn</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Downtown Ald. Brendan Reilly (42nd) reminded Roberts that Chicago has “gone more than two years without gunshot detection” and that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/editorials/2025/02/18/shotspotter-mayor-johnson-gunshot-detection-police-technology-city-hall" >bids to replace the technology</a> formerly provided by ShotSpotter “came in 18 months ago.” Instead of choosing a replacement, Johnson announced a "no-bid pilot," Reilly said.</p><p>It’s been three years since Johnson honored a campaign promise to progressive supporters by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/02/13/mayor-johnson-to-end-shotspotter-deal-after-summer" >canceling the city’s contract</a> with ShotSpotter, which he derisively called a “walkie-talkie on a stick.”</p><p>Johnson and his progressive supporters viewed the technology as costly, ineffective and a contributor to overpolicing in Black and Brown communities, where the majority of gun violence occurs.</p><p>Afterward, the Council empowered then-Chicago Police Supt. Larry Snelling to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2024/05/22/shotspotter-contract-wards-council-members-brandon-johnson-police-shootings-adam-toledo" >sign a new contract with ShotSpotter</a>. But Johnson declared the ordinance illegal, even after negotiating a costly extension to retain the technology through the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago.</p><p>Johnson then launched an open competition to replace ShotSpotter. SoundThinking was one of 15 firms responding to a request for information and one of nine companies responding to a follow-up request for proposals.</p><p>Ald. Gilbert Villegas (36th) asked about the testing of gunshot-detection technologies during the bidding process — a process Roberts initially couldn't recall. She eventually characterized the tests as "demonstrations" in a controlled environment and said the pilot would allow for a better analysis.</p><p>Roberts was a no-show at another recent hearing. She infuriated Council members by sending a letter informing them the pilot program was about to begin in six police districts: Wentworth, Calumet, Englewood, Deering, Ogden and Harrison.</p><p>Against that backdrop, the nonbinding referendum garnered 72% support. On the day after the election, Johnson hinted strongly that he would not be moved by the overwhelming vote.</p><p>“I support technology, but it has to be technology that is credible. It has to be technology that’s actually effective. It has to be technology that safeguards our community from anything that could be detrimental to our privacy. So I’ve put forth a pilot," Johnson said then.</p><p>When Roberts first disclosed the mayor's change of heart, she had trouble explaining it, and Budget Chair Jason Ervin (28th) had difficulty understanding what she was trying to say.</p><p>“What’s that mean in English?” Ervin asked Roberts.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/04/shotspotter-advisory-referendum-gunshot-detection-technology-brandon-johnson-opposition" >Most Chicago voters said they want ShotSpotter back, but that’s unlikely to sway Mayor Johnson</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/02/13/mayor-johnson-to-end-shotspotter-deal-after-summer" >Mayor Johnson to end ShotSpotter deal after summer, making good on key campaign promise</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/editorials/2025/02/18/shotspotter-mayor-johnson-gunshot-detection-police-technology-city-hall" >Will search for new gunshot detection system lead back to ShotSpotter?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Got a Thanksgiving holiday travel hack? We want to hear from you
entries.summary: <p>Thanksgiving is the busiest travel period of the year. </p><p>Last year, U.S. airports recorded their <a class="Link" href="https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-screened-record-313-million-airline-passengers-sunday-2025-12-01/" target="_blank" >busiest day ever</a> (on the Sunday after Thanksgiving). Amtrak <a class="Link" href="https://media.amtrak.com/2026/11/amtrak-encourages-travelers-to-book-thanksgiving-travel-early-amid-historic-demand/" target="_blank" >handled</a> its largest passengers volume ever. And more people are <a class="Link" href="https://newsroom.aaa.com/2025/11/aaa-thanksgiving-travel-forecast-2025/" target="_blank" >traveling by car</a> than before the COVID-19 pandemic.</p><p>With congestion worse than ever, the Chicago Sun-Times wants to hear your hacks for traveling during Thanksgiving. entries.title: Bills top punchless Vikings on ‘‘Monday Night Football’’
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS — Josh Allen threw a touchdown pass with 44 seconds left before halftime, James Cook rushed 31 times for 107 yards and a late score, and the Buffalo Bills beat Minnesota 23-6 on Monday night, sending Vikings deeper into their unrelenting offensive slump.</p><p>Linebackers Terrel Bernard and Dorian Williams had interceptions and Tyler Bass made three field goals to stretch his franchise-record streak to 24 straight as the Bills (7-1) matched their best eight-game start since 1993. That season ended with their last of four straight Super Bowl losses.</p><p>With Kyler Murray sidelined by a hamstring injury, Carson Wentz started at quarterback for the Vikings (6-2) and didn't finish what became one of the worst performances of his 11-year career. Wentz went 8 for 25 for 81 yards and three turnovers, including a backward pass in the first quarter that was thrown too high for even Justin Jefferson to catch it — resulting in a lost fumble near midfield.</p><p>Wentz, who was checked out in the medical tent at one point for an apparent lower leg injury, was replaced by Max Brosmer midway through the fourth quarter. Wentz completed 1 of 8 passes in the second half.</p><p>The battle of Buffalo's highest-scoring offense in the league against the least-scored-on defense might well have gone to Minnesota had the offense been able to muster a decent drive or two.</p><p>But the Vikings had four straight possessions in the first half start beyond their 40-yard line, and the furthest they made it was the Bills 48.</p><p>The Vikings as usual sent blitzers at Allen from every angle possible, recording four sacks and an interception of a heave into the end zone that Byron Murphy ran down and returned 55 yards. But the Bills eked out just enough in the first half to give themselves a cushion, when Allen found tight end Keleki Latu open in the back of the end zone for a 25-yard touchdown as he rolled right and was hit hard by Andrew Van Ginkel.</p><h3><b>Allen matches Manning’s 10-year touchdown mark</b></h3><p>With 322 regular-season touchdowns — 232 passing, 88 rushing and two receiving — Allen tied Peyton Manning for the most in NFL history over a player's first 10 years. Allen is halfway through his ninth season.</p><h3><b>Injury report</b></h3><p>Bills: Starting LT Dion Dawkins (ribs) and starting LG Alec Anderson (ankle) were inactive.</p><p>Vikings: WR Jauan Jennings (calf) and FS Theo Jackson (quadriceps) were inactive.</p>

entries.title: Employee hospitalized after break-in at Avondale restaurant
entries.summary: <p>An employee was hospitalized after a break-in at an Avondale restaurant Monday morning, according to police and media reports.</p><p>The break-in happened around 4:30 a.m. at Brothers Restaurant, 3000 W. Belmont Ave., multiple outlets reported. A man broke the front window and entered the building, displayed a sharp object and demanded money, police said.</p><p>Two employees inside the restaurant fought with the suspect, who pepper-sprayed them before taking money and running away. Co-owner Laura Villegas <a class="Link" href="https://wgntv.com/news/chicagocrime/avondale-restaurant-owner-employee-attacked-during-early-morning-break-in/" target="_blank" >told WGN-TV</a> her husband and the cook were involved in the fight.</p><p>“He was unconscious,” Villegas said. “My husband was afraid of his life, so he just throw the money, he said, ‘Here. There’s no more. I don’t have no more money. Just take it and go, take it and go."</p><p>The cook was taken to Swedish Hospital in fair condition. Villegas' husband refused medical treatment.</p><p>Detectives are investigating. No one is in custody.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Mom doesn't want to hear daughter's marriage gripes
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My adult daughter wants to confide (complain) to me about her husband — his quirky behavior, things he does that she doesn't like, etc. — nothing heavy or abusive. I have told her that I think it's inappropriate for her to talk to me about him, unfair to me and bad for the ongoing relationship I have with him.</p><p>Instead, she's confiding in my husband. I have told them both that maybe she should talk to her friends and therapist, since she has one. She responded: "All of my friends talk to their parents about their husbands and get their advice. Usually, they talk to their moms, but since you won't listen, I talk to Dad."</p><p>Am I wrong in thinking that a wife's strongest relationship should be with her husband, and that it is disloyal to speak to her parents about nonthreatening aggravations? I never spoke to my parents about my marriage, though there was plenty I could have shared! Have the rules changed? — <i>HEAR NO EVIL</i></p><p><b>DEAR HEAR NO EVIL:</b> I'm not sure there ever were any universal rules about this. Each family handles it in a way that works for them. If you dislike being your daughter's marriage adviser but your husband doesn't mind, I'd say they've hit upon the best solution for all involved. However, because you don't want to hear it, it would be best if they avoid holding their counseling sessions in your presence.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My sweet husband has a bad habit that I cannot correct. He goes into a room, pantry or closet and will not turn off the lights when he exits. I then go into a room or closet and find the lights on, and he hasn't been in there for 30 minutes. He says it's no big deal. I say it's wasting electricity and money! What say you? — <i>THRIFTY IN TEXAS</i></p><p><b>DEAR THRIFTY:</b> I say you two could save yourselves money and have fewer arguments if you buy motion-sensing light switches that operate automatically.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My son, 47, informed me in January that he and his wife of 13 years are divorcing. (She initiated the divorce.) When he proposed to her, he gave her my engagement ring from my late husband. About a year ago, I gave her an additional diamond-and-emerald band because I felt comfortable that the marriage was solid. I would like my rings back now. Am I out of line? — <i>GIVE ME A RING</i></p><p><b>DEAR GIVE ME A RING:</b> You did not mention whether the couple has any children. If they do, the heirloom ring should be set aside and given to one of them at an appropriate age. If not, the rules of etiquette dictate that it be returned to you. (Please note: Because an engagement ring is usually considered a gift to the intended, the rule of law may not agree with what is ethical and proper.)</p><p>The additional band you gave her isn't covered by the same rule of etiquette, but if you ask her nicely, she may be willing to return it.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Chicago’s South Side used to be a hub for Black theater. There’s hope it could flourish again.
entries.summary: <p>Built in 1897, the Forum Hall in Bronzeville may appear to be in a state of disrepair. But the venue, a staple of the 1950s-era Black Metropolis, is on the precipice of a return.</p><p>Today, developer Bernard Loyd is working to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/museums/2026/10/05/bronzeville-cultural-zone-museums-arts-black-history-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>revitalize the Forum</u></a> and has already brought musicians back to the space. This fall Perceptions Theater and Coalescence Theatre Project will stage Kelundra Smith’s “Other Paths to God,” at Definition.</p><p>A short walk away, Court Theatre, located on the U. of C. campus, has become one of the premiere Equity venues in the city — recently doing more to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/08/06/free-court-theatre-history-black-playwrights-ron-oj-parson-chuck-smith-series-south-side" target="_blank" ><u>showcase the work of Black artists</u></a> than it has in the past. The Beverly Arts Center, founded in 1967, remains the home of resident company Beverly Theatre Guild, the oldest community theater company in Chicago.</p><p>And while it’s not a Black-led company, Locals, including developer Bernard Loyd (seen here at the Forum in Bronzeville), hope that a new chapter might be emerging. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Victor Hilitski for the Chicago Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Theaters suffered a double whammy,” said Loyd. “One is that 75% of the population left, and therefore there was no local population to feed these theaters.” The new laws allowed Black audiences into venues like the Chicago Theatre downtown, so the remaining residents could travel out of the neighborhood to see plays.</p><p>Now, South Side theater seems to be on the rise once again. Theater makers say they are intent to push forward, while also being mindful about connecting the future of South Side theater to its glorious past.</p><p>“We’re building on land Lorraine Hansberry used to own,” said Definition’s Phillips. “That’s part of plugging into legacy, of knowing how our stories can affect our real lives — that's why we're in it.”</p>

entries.title: Where to eat in drink in Chicago’s West Town
entries.summary: <p>In recent years, buzz has steadily grown that Chicago crowned a new Restaurant Row, toppling the long-dominant Randolph Street in the West Loop. Just northwest of the West Loop’s corporate glass towers and slick restaurants, West Town, the low-slung, still (somewhat) affordable, concrete and brick neighborhood houses a slew of restaurant and bar hot spots, several earning nods from the kingmaking Michelin Guide and James Beard Foundation. Price per square foot — averaging between <a class="Link" href="https://chicagobroker.com/west-loop-fulton-market-office-space/" target="_blank" ><u>$50 and $85</u></a> in high-visibility areas of the West Loop compared to West Town, where it more <a class="Link" href="https://www.loopnet.com/search/restaurants/west-town-chicago-il/for-lease/" target="_blank" ><u>typically</u></a> runs between $30 and $50 — undoubtedly played a role in the latter’s ascent, as hotly anticipated indie outfits opt to set up shop here, from Pizz’Amici, Bar Bambi and Guillotine Bakery to Feld and Gilda.</p><p> Time Out all but cemented the neighborhood’s It status in September, when it deemed it the <a class="Link" href="https://www.timeout.com/chicago/news/this-chicago-neighborhood-was-just-named-one-of-the-worlds-coolest-ranking-higher-than-places-in-new-york-paris-and-amsterdam-091626" target="_blank" ><u>18th “coolest” neighborhood in the world</u></a> — joining Chinatown in Los Angeles (No. 4) and New York’s Financial District (No. 28) as the only U.S. cities on the list. “On-the-ground experts" purportedly determined this by weighing food and drink, nightlife, unique local businesses, liveability and community.  </p><p>Those in the know consider this old news. Brunch stalwart Flo (closing on Dec. 20) brought New Mexican classics like sopapillas and hatch green chicken chile stew to Chicago Avenue well before the borderlands got its culinary due, as beloved breakfast spot Uncle Mike’s Place did for homespun Filipino-American cooking. Coalfire put artisanal Neapolitan pizza on the map years before thin-crust pizza joint Pizz’Amici opened a few doors down and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/food-drink/2025/10/21/tavern-pizza-chicago-grand-avenue-pizzamici-coalfire-salernos" target="_blank" ><u>became the hottest table in town</u></a>, cementing Grand Avenue as Chicago's pizza highway.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-770000" Michelin-starred modern Filipino restaurant Kasama (two stars) and hyperseasonal tasting menu spot Feld (one star), both received the best regional chef James Beard Foundation Award (JBFA): Kasama in 2023, Feld <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/food-drink/2026/06/15/james-beard-awards-2026-chicago-lyric-opera-chefs-restaurant" target="_blank" ><u>this year</u></a>. Spanish-leaning JBFA semifinalist Bocadillo Market lives here, as does Michelin Guide-recognized Korean tasting menu Jeong, plus Jean Banchet Award darlings Brasero, chef John Manion’s South American restaurant and bar, and Flour Power, the counter-service scratch pasta joint from former Schwa chef de cuisine Wilson Bauer. Indeed, if a neighborhood’s proverbial arrival is judged by its chef quibbles, West Town made it official this summer. Bauer beefed with Feld’s very online chef/owner Jake Potashnick over unfounded claims about the latter’s ingredient sourcing. Maybe it’s to be expected when one restaurant self-describes as <a class="Link" href="https://www.flourpowerpasta.com/extras" target="_blank" ><u>“terpene to table”</u></a> and the other <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/food-drink/2026/06/10/feld-restaurant-chicago-michelin-james-beard-jake-potashnick" target="_blank" ><u>“relationship to table.”</u></a><u> </u></p><p>So what’s all the fuss about West Town? Your faithful food and drink reporter took a companion along to spend consecutive Friday nights in October on a mile-long stretch of Chicago Avenue, the neighborhood’s beating heart for restaurants and nightlife. We visited almost a dozen spots, for which I made only one reservation. We sampled Latin American happy hour bites and traded tequila shots for mini Polaroids. We glimpsed matcha’s photogenic grip on Gen Z, tasted pan-cultural pintxos and authentic Isaan street food, and trendspotted martinis from freezer-cold to carbonated, bracingly clean to filthy. Here’s your Friday night itinerary in West Town.</p><p><b>5:15 p.m.: Snack (attempt) at Lao Peng You and Dell’ Rooster happy hour</b></p><p>It’s mild and sunny when I hop off my bike around Chicago and Damen Avenues. <a class="Link" href="https://www.oldfriendchicago.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Lao Peng You</u></b></a>’s, 2020 W. Chicago Ave., tiny sidewalk patio is packed with a youngish crowd slurping cold chicken, oil-slicked dumplings and steamy noodles. Judging by the line, my plan to grab a takeaway dumpling snack will not pan out. Nor would I bother trying my luck for a table at its high-profile next-door neighbor, <a class="Link" href="https://www.feldrestaurant.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Feld Restaurant</u></b></a>, 2018 W. Chicago Ave. I learned from Potashnick that as of Oct. 9, his restaurant is booked up through the end of November, with two-thirds of December tables spoken for. That is, unless you’re an aspiring chef. Each Saturday, Feld reserves a pair of seats for free dinner for culinary students.</p><p>Anyway, I have to hurry if I’m going to catch happy hour at <a class="Link" href="https://dellrooster.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Dell’ Rooster Restaurant & Bar</u></b></a>, 1825 W. Chicago Ave., which ends at 6 p.m. Every day starting at 3, this upbeat, Latin-owned restaurant serves juicy Mango Caribeños rimmed in puckering Tajin and bracing margaritas for $9 and beers for $4. I’m surprised to see the place mostly empty — in this economy! Tender empanadas ($8) pack a satisfying bite of sweet corn and mild chihuahua cheese atop zingy chipotle aioli.</p><p><b>6:30 p.m.: Gen Z watching at Match | A and date-night happy hour at Brasero</b></p><p>West Town’s hottest bar is … <a class="Link" href="https://www.finditmatch-a.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Match | A</u></b></a>, 1857 W. Chicago Ave. One might think so, anyway, given how packed this minichain (open til 8 p.m.) is with twentysomethings, perusing matcha merch or draped over curved cement seating by the front window sipping frothed, cream-topped, multicolored matcha drinks. Touchscreens abound in the minimalist cafe whose counter is lined with black chawan bowls. Alas, the ASMR of handwhisking matcha is overshadowed by a blaring soundtrack of Dua Lipa and Kidz Bop Kids. My two-toned, sweetened iced matcha is delicious, layering kelly-green, umami-rich matcha atop mildly sugared green tea.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" vibes and shots at Golden Years</b></p><p> At this still-early hour, one might nab a bar seat after a short wait at the pretty, plant-filled <a class="Link" href="https://www.barnettare.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Nettare</u></a>, 1953 W. Chicago Ave., a Midwestern-centric restaurant and bottle shop. Sade croons to tables full of group dates digging into Illinois-raised pork rillettes and wagyu aguachile with fermented peppers. The extensive cocktail menu includes tiny but potent “Small Sips” for $8 or $9, including an autumnal, bittersweet apple brandy and fermented rhubarb cocktail, or the Chicago White Negroni, with Old Tom gin, Malort and vermouth, which starts softly botanical before giving way to a bitter hall of mirrors.  </p><p>A handful of open tables likewise remain at <a class="Link" href="https://www.goldenyearschicago.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Golden Years</u></b></a>, 1938 W. Chicago Ave., the easygoing, 1970s-inspired cocktail joint in the bygone home of High Dive. The turmeric-stained Ginger Fizz, with black and white rum, sugared Swedish Punsch rum liqueur and lime, almost convinces me it’s a health cocktail. (At $13.75, it’s practically happy hour pricing — in this economy!). The crowd leans youngish, tables full of thirtysomething friends and couples looking too at ease for a first date. We snack on sticky, savory bacon-wrapped dates laced with goat cheese while debating the Group Shot, a $6 combo of bourbon or tequila plus one Polaroid. Should you relinquish the photo, your grimacing shot face joins countless others lining the wall en route to the bathroom.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-800000" name="image-800000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6503ee7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2Fa0%2Fe374186f4f398a925122ab7b74cd%2Fwesttownfood-261111-9.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d02f971/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2Fa0%2Fe374186f4f398a925122ab7b74cd%2Fwesttownfood-261111-9.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/37b4ea6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2Fa0%2Fe374186f4f398a925122ab7b74cd%2Fwesttownfood-261111-9.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The Hamburger, fries, and onion rings with a Coors Golden Banquet, served at Golden Years located at 1938 W. Thai or book ahead for Gilda pintxos</b></p><p>The desire for real sustenance growls its disapproval in my stomach. Thankfully, the early dinner rush at <a class="Link" href="https://www.jjthaistreetfood.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>J.J. Thai Street Food</u></b></a>, 1715 W. Chicago Ave., has thinned enough that we’re swept to a booth without waiting at this homey, wood-walled joint that chef and owner Jiranya "Jina" Thosatheppitak opened in 2015. The nam tok neua yang (beef salad) — teeming with charred ribeye, mint leaves, sliced onion, lime, chiles and nutty roasted rice powder — is textural, bright and umami-rich. We can’t resist an order of khao pad phoo (crab fried rice). White pepper supercharges the gentle brackish funk of sweet lump crab, which mingles with egg, green onion and toothsome rice; we season liberally with accompanying Thai chiles in fish sauce. We’re too full for the excellent, milky-sweet mango sticky rice, and call it an early night after a few good hours of imbibing. Back home, I’m grateful we’d ordered the sticky rice to go.</p><p>The following Friday, I head to <a class="Link" href="https://gildarestaurant.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Gilda</u></b></a>, 1421 W. Chicago Ave. for dinner, thanking past me for having the foresight to reserve a table a few weeks in advance. This diminutive indie taberna, bootstrapped with help from an unconventional community investment campaign, tingles with energy. The Gilda (namesake speared tapa trio of anchovy, pickled chile and olive) adorns the anchovy-boosted Lady Gilda (dirty martini) that alights on nearly every table, like a gnarled, Seussian mascot. Servers throw their emotional weight behind their favorites on this fleeting, Basque(ish) menu. Crunchy-then-rich BBQ eel croquetas with sweet-savory Japanese tare aioli, and the best tortilla española I’ve had outside Spain: custardy and rich, naughtily draped in garlicky hollandaise.</p><div Chicago Ave., swearing I saw a pile of dirty snow <i>inside</i>. Artist Tony Tasset’s year-round <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/dca/supp_info/chicago_s_publicarttonytassetssnowsculptureforchicago.html" target="_blank" ><u>sculpture</u></a> of a plowed pile of snow, complete with handcrafted grayish grime and trash, represents a fitting last display for the old department store and a beautifully ugly reminder of the long, dark city winter that’s always coming.  </p><p>Walking into <a class="Link" href="https://www.bambichicago.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Bar Bambi</u></b></a>, 1703 W. Chicago Ave., after dark feels a little like entering a neon-tinted runway show; I’m relieved I like my fit. This immersive spot from bartender and first-time owner/operator Katie Renshaw mingles geometric accents, conversation pit-style couches and bold houndstooth patterns beneath sculptural color-changing neons. We perch at a long, low couch by the entrance over the Context Clues, a sprightly dirty martini highball tinged with celery brine, sherry and coriander. Every cocktail here feels fresh and a bit cheeky. Consider the Secret Handshake, a fruity, chocolate-scented Sazerac with cognac and rye whiskey, nutella, cherry vinegar and absinthe, or the gently peaty (N/A) Magic Conch milk punch with pineapple, toasted coconut and cardamom. If peckish, might I suggest the naughty eggs with Calabrian chile and dill chip crumbles or the salmon crudo with toasted rice and nuoc cham?</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div beam, our feet find their way to 16 On Center’s nightclub stalwart <a class="Link" href="https://www.beautybarchicago.com/" target="_blank" ><b>Beauty Bar</b></a>, 1444 W. Chicago Ave. As with most nights, there’s no cover tonight. Cowboy boots and braids are, seemingly, back in sartorial force and the ubiquity of every flavor of High Noon nods to the summer-like weather outside. (Or maybe it never goes out of season on the dance floor.) The uncommitted shoulder bouncers collide with self-assured full-body swayers in timeless fashion. entries.title: Scooter driver fatally shoots man in Little Village over weekend, police say
entries.summary: <p>The death of a man who was shot by a person riding a scooter in Little Village Saturday night was ruled a homicide.</p><p>The unidentified 34-year-old man was standing outside in the 3100 block of South Kolin Avenue around 11:10 p.m. Saturday when he was shot in the head by someone on a dark-colored moped, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital where he died, police said. </p><p>A Monday autopsy determined he died of multiple gunshot wounds and his death was ruled a homicide, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>Area 4 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Votes for Chicago's first fully elected school board are in. What you need to know about all 21 races.
entries.summary: <p>Chicagoans made history Tuesday as they cast their ballots for all 21 members of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/" target="_blank" ><u>city’s school board</u></a> for the first time.</p><p>The showdown for the school board was the marquee race on the ballot, with Gov. JB Pritzker easily winning a third term and Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton securing retiring U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin’s seat.</p><p>Many had their eye on the citywide race for school board president — a powerful position that sets the board’s agenda and, until now, has never been elected. Sitting school board member <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/jessica-biggs/" target="_blank" ><u>Jessica Biggs</u></a> won that race, besting her two opponents, the Chicago Teachers Union-backed <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/hilario-dominguez/" target="_blank" ><u>Hilario Dominguez</u></a> and prominent defense attorney <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/victor-p-henderson/" target="_blank" ><u>Victor Henderson</u></a>.</p><p>Political action committees and individuals <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>funneled more than $5.2 million</u></a> into that heated three-way race.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/11/03/chicago-teachers-union-poised-to-capture-half-of-school-board-district-seats-but-likely-to-lose-presidency" >balance of power</a> on the school board could be a harbinger of February’s mayoral race. Mayor Brandon Johnson, a close ally of the CTU, is running for reelection and appointed the majority of current school board members. As of Wednesday morning, candidates backed by the CTU had won seven of the 20 district races and were leading in three races that were too close to call. entries.title: Man fatally shoots himself as authorities tried to arrest him in Back of the Yards: police
entries.summary: <p>An autopsy is scheduled Tuesday for a man who allegedly fatally shot himself as authorities tried to arrest him Monday morning in the Back of the Yards on the South Side, police said. </p><p>Members of the U.S. Marshals Great Lakes Regional Fugitive Task Force, which includes Chicago Police officers, were preparing to serve an arrest warrant at a home in the 5400 block of South Hermitage Avenue around 9:35 a.m. Monday when the 53-year-old man who was the subject of the warrant shot himself in the head, police said. </p><p>The unidentified man was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where he was pronounced dead about an hour later, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>An autopsy to determine the cause and manner of his death is scheduled, the medical examiner's office said. </p><p>A weapon was recovered at the scene and no officers fired their weapons, officials said. </p><p>The Investigative Response Team is investigating.</p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydhtpky-l-th/" target="_blank" >Mitch Dudek</a></h5><p>If ever there was an underdog Chicago could get behind, Rupert Cintron is it.</p><p>Cintron, an Elgin-based truck driver and father of four, made his debut as a pro sumo wrestler in a new league that swung through Chicago over the weekend.</p><p>"It's just an opportunity at my age to be able to do something like this," Cintron told the Sun-Times last week. "I'm 51 years old, and I'm about to get out there with these kids, and, you know, it's just cool. ... It's like life never ends if you don’t let the dream end. Just keep going."</p><p>With little sumo experience to his name, Cintron is very much just a dude in the right place and time who was given a shot. He hasn't worked out — in a gym, at least — in seven years. But every day, he moves about 11,000 pounds of flour, beef and other raw materials from his truck into the basements of Chicago restaurants.</p><p>At 5 feet 10 inches and 260 pounds, Cintron is also very green when it comes to sumo. He began wrestling only two years ago and is still learning all the Japanese words that go hand-in-hand with the sport, which Americans tend to pick up as adults. Professional Japanese sumo wrestlers typically start learning the sport at a young age.</p><p>We tagged along with Cintron as he competed in his debut match on Saturday.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydhtpky-l-tk/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p>Thanksgiving is the busiest travel period of the year.</p><p><b>With congestion worse than ever, the Sun-Times wants to hear your hacks for traveling during Thanksgiving. entries.title: Morgan Park students walk out of school in support of fired football coach Chris James
entries.summary: <p>A couple hundred Morgan Park students walked out of class on Tuesday to protest the school’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/11/09/morgan-park-fires-football-coach-chris-james" >firing of football coach Chris James</a>. Parents and family members held an impromptu press conference detailing their frustrations with the decision.</p><p>“We just stand with Chris,” said Chris Mathews, the uncle of football player Travezz Jones. “We don’t know the ins and outs of it. Even if Chris were to go to another school for another opportunity, he deserves that grace. He did so much for this school that he should be able to leave with his dignity, his pride. He should be able to walk out of the door with his head held high.”</p><p>Morgan Park principal Dan Kuzma fired James on Monday. James told the Sun-Times it was because he wouldn’t immediately commit to coaching the Mustangs next season. Kuzma disputed that, saying there was more to it.</p><p>Chicago Public Schools declined to comment further, simply forwarding the message Kuzma sent to Morgan Park football families on Monday.</p><p>James, a Morgan Park grad and beloved member of the school’s community, has been the head football coach for nine seasons. He’s built the best football program in the Public League.</p><p>“[James] has literal players in college making hundreds of thousands a year after coming from the South Side of Chicago,” Mathews said. “He has done so much for this community. We stand with Chris throughout whatever. And he is an alumni. And then you don’t let the kids finish their season? They fought hard all year for this.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c00000" Winning at the statewide level at a CPS school is extremely difficult. Morgan Park doesn’t have a football stadium, and its sports budget for coaches and equipment lags far behind suburban schools.</p><p>Still, the immediate firing and cancellation of the rest of the season means the team can’t compete in the Public League playoffs, a consolation tournament where the winner earns a spot in the Prep Bowl against the top consolation-bracket Catholic League team.</p><p>“We are devastated that he is not going to be able to play in the Prep Bowl,” said Tiffany Burnett, the mother of junior football player Rashad Burnett. “My son is concerned about what he is going to do for his senior year. He was looking forward to playing for CJ his senior year. Now we are looking at having to transfer or go to another school with a better sports program. We understand athletics may not be everything, but they are for some children. We are just asking for answers.”</p><p>James released another statement on Tuesday:</p><p>“The administration at Morgan Park, led by [Kuzma] has done a great job at MP. Just because we disagree on football or athletics, please do not discredit the work they have done and the work of everyone at “1744” to make a difference every day….I do not care to discuss details publicly because I do not want this to get in the way of developing the children of our community. I strongly urge you to continue to support the students at Morgan Park High School, they need you more than ever.”</p><p>James’ statement ends with a plea for the school to restore access to the football team’s Hudl account. Hudl records high school football games, and players and coaches use it to assemble highlight videos to send to colleges.</p><p>“My son needs his footage so he can go to college,” said Tia Benjamin, the mother of junior football player Milen Porter. “He wants to be a Bison, he wants to go to NDSU. Some of these kids already have their scholarships, but not all of them.”</p>

entries.title: White Sox moving relief ace Grant Taylor to the rotation, Hagen Smith will remain in the bullpen
entries.summary: <p>LAS VEGAS – It’s unclear if he crossed the threshold specifically while he was throwing four innings in Game 1 of the American League Division Series, but Grant Taylor has shown the work capacity for the White Sox to believe he’s ready for a step up from the bullpen.</p><p>The Sox are moving their relief ace to the starting rotation for 2027 the season, which general manager Chris Getz first announced in an MLB Network interview on Monday night. Left-hander Hagen Smith will remain in the bullpen, where he impressed (1.29 ERA, 41 K in 28 IP) after being called up in August.</p><p>The 24-year-old Taylor was dominant in his first full year in the majors, striking out 106 batters in 84 innings of relief during the regular season and posting a 2.25 ERA. He logged another 8 ⅔ innings of work during a White Sox postseason run where the team relied on Taylor as their top option. The right-hander told the Sun-Times that workload put him squarely in the middle of the 85 to 100-inning range he and the team set as a preseason goal to build up toward starting.</p><p>With a high-90s fastball that features unique riding action and a suite of breaking balls, Taylor has the sort of impact stuff the Sox rotation lacked outside the best stretches of Sean Burke. But with Taylor’s past injury history and light track record for logging heavy innings, the team is still pursuing starting pitching as a top priority.</p><p>They now need someone to step up and replace their most trusted reliever of the 2026 season as well.</p>

entries.title: Moped driver fatally shoots man in Little Village over weekend, police say
entries.summary: <p>The death of a man who was shot by a person riding a scooter in Little Village Saturday night was ruled a homicide.</p><p>The unidentified 34-year-old man was standing outside in the 3100 block of South Kolin Avenue around 11:10 p.m. Saturday when he was shot in the head by someone on a dark-colored moped, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital where he died, police said. </p><p>A Monday autopsy determined he died of multiple gunshot wounds and his death was ruled a homicide, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>Area 4 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: As America observes Veterans Day, Pete Hegseth picks which vets to honor — and which to abuse
entries.summary: <p>Wednesday is Veterans Day — originally Armistice Day, begun in 1919 for the first anniversary of the end of World War I, which wasn't called that at the time, since nobody knew another was coming. It was called "The Great War" or "The World War." </p><p>The first Armistice Day was a dramatic moment in Chicago — at 10:55 a.m. on Nov. 11, 1919, soldiers in Grant Park let off a fusillade of artillery and small arms fire, promptly stopping at 11 a.m. — the war had ended, famously, at the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month. Cops paused Loop traffic. 'L' cars stopped. A full minute's silence, then a cheer went up and LaSalle Street became a blizzard of confetti.</p><p>Armistice Day became Veterans Day in 1954, acknowledging the millions of Americans who had served in World War II and the Korean War.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-420000" name="module-420000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>There is no possessive in Veterans Day — it isn't "Veterans' Day" — for the simple reason the day does not belong to them, but to us. It is a time when the American public is supposed to reflect on our debt to those who served our country. (And are still alive; we honor the fallen on Memorial Day).</p><p>But which veterans should we honor? Do Black veterans count? Blacks have served since the Revolutionary War, but the Army wasn't integrated until 1948. This was done over the objections of the brass, such as Army Chief of Staff General Omar Bradley, who argued that mixing races would lower morale, hurt unit cohesion, and turn the military into a social experiment rather than a fighting force.</p><p>This wasn't accepted by President Harry Truman, nauseated by the horrific abuse that Black soldiers suffered when they returned home to the segregated South, which instead of honoring Black vets often brutalized them for the crime of wearing crisp uniforms and holding themselves with pride.</p><p>Truman said he was from Missouri, and his forebears were Confederates, but: "my very stomach turned over when I learned that Negro soldiers just back from overseas, were being dumped out of arm trucks in Mississippi and beaten. Whatever my inclinations as a native of Missouri might have been, as President, I know this is bad. I shall fight evils like this."</p><p>He did, by desegregating the military. But what one president giveth, another may take away. Donald Trump's secretary of war, Pete Hegseth, has waged an open battle against Black service members, blocking or stalling promotions of Black and female senior officers, claiming any advancement had to be due to DEI rather than merit. Others have been dismissed or forced into retirement. Online tributes to historic Black service members have been taken down while books by Black authors were removed from military academy libraries.</p><p>The Jim Crow arguments against a desegregated military were retrofitted for use against trans troops. The week he took office for his second term, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14183, “Prioritizing Military Excellence and Readiness,” banning transgender and nonbinary service members from the military, where thousands serve with honor. The order baselessly slurs trans troops as lacking the "selflessness and humility" needed to serve our country.</p><p>There is good news. Procedures are big in the military, and in order to cashier conscientious trans soldiers, sailors and marines, the government set up a series of three-person "separation boards" to throw them out.</p><p>Only the boards are refusing. Judging their buddies based on their merits, and not blind prejudice, they decline to dismiss them. The whole thing is secret, but a <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/us/trans-troops-military-boards-retain.html" target="_blank" >New York Times investigation </a>found that, more often than not, the boards keep their comrades.</p><p>"The votes are a stunning rebuke from the armed forces, where following orders is bedrock," the Times wrote. "And they suggest the military’s transgender ban is being rejected by the very troops the administration says the ban is meant to serve."</p><p>Freedom is not free. Someone always pays a price. At Veterans Day 2026, we should remember that most military personnel never see battle. But that does not mean they do not have an opportunity to courageously fight for America. When the story of this shameful era becomes history, there will be flashy, dramatic moments, such as ordinary citizens turning out — like the Minutemen of old — to oppose masked ICE thugs in the street. There will be heroic soldiers like Gen. Mark A. Milley, who placed love of country over selfish concerns and stood up for the Constitution and human dignity. And there are nameless officers on secret panels who declined to reject their fellow jarheads and swabbies simply because of who they are. The debt that civilians owe the military is always deep. But lately it has compounded, in our ongoing battles against enemies both foreign <i>and</i> domestic.</p>
entries.author: Neil Steinberg

entries.title: Will the Illinois House elect its first woman speaker? Dems float potential contenders to replace Welch
entries.summary: <p>After this week’s bombshell announcement that Illinois’ first Black House speaker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/11/05/illinois-house-speaker-chris-welch-mutiny-26-democrats-call-for-new-leader-harry-benton-scandal" target="_blank" ><u>wouldn’t seek a fourth term</u></a>, Democratic state legislators could blaze another new trail with their selection for the next leader of their chamber.</p><p>Five women lawmakers were among the names floated most frequently as the Sun-Times spoke on background with more than a dozen lawmakers, lobbyists and other insiders sizing up potential candidates to replace outgoing House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch, D-Hillside.</p><p>Many said it was time for Illinois to see its first woman speaker to help uproot an entrenched culture of sexual harassment following the Capitol’s latest scandal.</p><p>Welch lost the support of most of his caucus in the wake of his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/05/welch-benton-harassment-working-group-cassidy" target="_blank" ><u>delayed response</u></a> to misconduct allegations against disgraced ex-state Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield — just like Welch’s longtime predecessor, imprisoned ex-Speaker Michael Madigan, was felled amid criticism of his inaction on complaints within his political organization.</p><p>There has scarcely been a question about the occupancy of the speaker’s office since Madigan first tightened his iron grip on the gavel in 1983. And even for a brief interlude of Republican House control in 1995-96, Lee Daniels was a clear pick to shift from GOP minority leader.</p><p>Now, for the first time in four decades, legislators have adequate time to seriously consider a field of representatives to step up in their chamber, without an incumbent or another obvious power player towering over the election for speaker.</p><p>Welch was a late entry in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/1/13/22228758/emanuel-chris-welch-illinois-house-speaker-vote-mike-madigan" target="_blank" ><u>the 2021 intra-party race</u></a> after Madigan’s stunning announcement he was stepping down, prompting <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/1/12/22227890/sources-latinx-caucus-latino-welch-hispanic-house-speaker-black-madigan-hernandez-williams-kifowit" target="_blank" ><u>a chaotic scramble for votes</u></a> over the final day of a lame-duck legislative session — a power grab that didn’t even play out in the Capitol itself. Lawmakers were masked and socially distanced in a Springfield convention center in the depths of the COVID-19 pandemic.</p><p>“By the time [Madigan] suspended his campaign, there were 24 hours for us to make a decision,” said North Side state Rep. Kelly Cassidy, one of the legislators who led the movement for new leadership. “That’s not a healthy way for us to do this.</p><p>“We have an actual chance to put thought into this that we didn’t get to before, and to hear from our colleagues about their visions. We have such an array of experience and talent throughout every corner of our caucus,” Cassidy said — noting she’s “not even remotely” interested in the post herself.</p><p>Asked if it’s time for a female speaker, Gov. JB Pritzker said “that's going to be up to the members.”</p><p>“What I know is that anybody who has been sexually harassed or had anything like that happen to them should know what the process is for reporting that,” Pritzker said at an unrelated news conference Friday. “The House is really responsible for getting their house in order… Every company, every nonprofit, virtually everybody I know, has developed a process for their institutions to deal with these things. It should be no different for the House of Representatives.”</p><p>Maneuvering behind closed doors will accelerate during the fall veto session that starts Nov. 17, reaching a political crescendo with the speaker's election in January immediately after the 105th General Assembly is sworn in.</p><p>The Sun-Times identified just one hat officially thrown into the ring by Friday morning, but plenty more will be in the weeks ahead. Here are eight names to watch, with more guaranteed to follow in the race for 60 votes:</p><h3>State Rep. Eva-Dina Delgado, D-Chicago</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a70000" name="image-a70000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9a61f73/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2Fc5%2Ff41de11f4fbebe22a20eb969d61a%2Ftransit-102424-6.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8efefc0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2Fc5%2Ff41de11f4fbebe22a20eb969d61a%2Ftransit-102424-6.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/263c9a6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2Fc5%2Ff41de11f4fbebe22a20eb969d61a%2Ftransit-102424-6.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="State Rep.
