entries.title: City Council’s aldermanic opposition demands that Mayor Johnson revamp his proposed budget
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson built his pre-election budget around a revival of his failed corporate head tax, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/28/city-council-opposition-pre-election-budget-battle-mayor-brandon-johnson" >defying a warning</a> from the City Council majority that rewrote his budget last year.</p><p>On Tuesday, 28 members of that same coalition drew an even wider line in the sand.</p><p>They informed Johnson his proposed <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/10/20/mayor-brandon-johnson-failed-corporate-head-tax-resurrected-proposed-budget" >$17.6 billion budget</a> does not have the votes to pass the Council for reasons that go far beyond the head tax, and it's up to him to rewrite his spending plan — they’re not going to do the work for him.</p><p>In a letter to the mayor delivered on the final day of City Council budget hearings, anti-administration alderpersons delivered a bill of particulars with six major items.</p><p>It starts with a $25-a-month, per-employee tax on businesses with more than 125 employees.</p><p>“You were told that a tax on jobs, which hinders our city’s ability to grow, would not get our votes. Yet, you put it in your budget anyway,” the letter states. “Taxing jobs prevents growth and moves the city in the wrong direction… Employers deciding where to expand can choose the suburbs or another state and every job that goes elsewhere takes with it the paychecks, spending and property taxes that makes up the city’s tax base.”</p><p>An even bigger-ticket item declared a non-starter is Johnson’s third, and biggest, increase in a Chicago tax on equipment rentals and cloud computing — already the highest such tax in the nation.</p><p>“Moving the rate from 15% to 20% is a tax increase on every Chicago business and individual who leases equipment or pays for cloud software — from the neighborhood restaurant renting its dishwashing machine and point-of sale system to the family renting equipment from the hardware store to clean out a flooded basement,” the letter states.</p><p>Last year, the management ordinance tied to the city’s 2026 budget called for no increase in that “cloud tax” for two years.</p><p>“We will not break our word on the cap we imposed last year," the letter states.</p><p>Acting Budget Director Jonathan Ernst has said the two-year freeze was stricken from the management ordinance because, “This is where the economy is moving toward, away from areas that we typically tax. We need to evolve with that."</p><p>The letter also claims nearly half the gap in Johnson’s budget was closed with “one-time money and borrowing that will not be there next year."</p><p>That includes the $75 million up-front payment from the New York investment firm that acquired Chicago parking meters; $37.7 million from the moribund Catalyst Fund; and $480 million in borrowing for settlements tied to police wrongdoing.</p><p>Johnson was further accused of leaving “billions of dollars owed to the city sitting on the books” and “adding tens of millions in new spending, while claiming $119.8 million in savings, but “itemizing none of it.” </p><p>“Aside from cutting police positions, your proposal appears to mostly shift recurring costs onto other city funds. That is cost shifting — not making government more efficient,” the letter states. “Growing spending in the middle of a $882 million budget gap is unfathomable, and every new dollar becomes a recurring cost with no plan to pay for it in future budgets.”</p><p>Johnson threw the political hot potato back into the laps of his Council opponents.</p><p>“No one has come up with a viable solution other than saying what they do not want. People have to come to the table saying what they do want. What are they willing to do?” he said.</p><p>If City Council members “like the investments” he’s making in mental health, sanitation services, libraries and youth jobs," they need to find a way to “fund them,” Johnson said.</p><p>He argued the blue wave that swept Democrats to victories across the nation was “not about cuts, consolidations, efficiencies and neo-liberal politics and austere budgets that have caused the fascist regime that we are experiencing now” from the Trump administration.</p><p>“The blue wave was about making sure that we are improving the quality of life for everyday people. We’re talking about basic human needs that people are calling for,” Johnson said Tuesday.</p><p>Last year, responding to Johnson's proposed spending plan, a 31-member coalition seized control over the budget process, long controlled by Chicago mayors, in ways not seen since the 1980’s power struggle known as “Council Wars.”</p><p>After rejecting Johnson’s corporate head tax, anti-administration Council members passed an alternative revenue package that the mayor opposed. This year, with three months to go before mayoral and aldermanic elections, the anti-administration group is not willing to do the heavy lifting again.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p>“We are telling you now with 51 days left before the City is required to have an approved budget so your team has ample time to write a budget that can earn the votes of this Council instead of spending the next several weeks defending one that cannot.”</p>
entries.author: Fran Spielman

entries.title: The Bears have problems, but are they as dramatic as those of the other presumed Super Bowl contenders?
entries.summary: <p>Three things I think I know about the 7-2 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>, who — “a win is a win” baloney aside — backed into a bye week with a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/08/bears-grades-buccaneers-caleb-williams-ben-johnson-chicago-sunday-night-soldier-field-nfl" target="_blank" >mistake-filled 27-24 near-disaster against the Buccaneers</a> at Soldier Field:</p><p><b>1. At least they have first-world problems: </b>Heading into Tuesday’s trade deadline, the Bears had a dearth of warm, healthy bodies in their defensive backfield. Their esteemed rushing attack is in a five-game relative lull, all without Kyle Monangai, as D’Andre Swift keeps taking hits. And then there’s the Caleb Williams question: Was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/09/bears-qb-caleb-williams-must-use-4-interception-game-vs-buccaneers-to-to-keep-growing" target="_blank" >an out-of-nowhere four-interception fiasco</a> just a meaningless one-off or are there cracks in the foundation?</p><p>But look around the league at some of the other leading teams and ask if you’d want the Bears to trade places. The Chiefs, for example, are 6-2, but quarterback Patrick Mahomes hasn’t completed a pass of at least 20 yards through the air since Week 4. Beardom would be up for grabs with frustration if Williams were dinking and dunking like the three-time Super Bowl MVP.</p><p>As potent as the 6-3 Packers’ passing game is — and it’s scary-good — they’re still the bottom-ranked rushing team in the NFL, and now they’ll be without Josh Jacobs for another, potentially lengthy stretch. The 6-2 Lions rank 32nd — dead last — against the pass. The 7-1 Bills, commonly viewed as the best team in the NFL, rank 29th against the pass even after winning easily Monday against the Vikings and QB Carson Wentz, who saw Williams’ Sunday-night meltdown and raised him a fat stack of pure incompetence.</p><p>And the 6-2 Vikings? Before reportedly dealing with the Raiders for old friend Kirk Cousins on Tuesday, they had easily the worst QB1 in the NFC North in Kyler Murray and a reputed QB-whisperer coach, Kevin O’Connell, who couldn’t count on his offense whatsoever. Cousins should be an upgrade, but he’s no Jared Goff, Jordan Love or Williams. This hardly means the Vikings are out of the woods.</p><p>We’re only halfway through the regular season — nine weeks down, nine to go — but some of those could be fatal flaws. The Bears’ flaws don’t seem as dramatic.</p><p><b>2. Turnovers? What turnovers? </b>After leading the NFL last season in both takeaways and fewest turnovers committed — to the tune of an unreal differential of plus-22 — the Bears have lost their mojo in this area. Their 17 giveaways are tied for third-most in the league. They’re the only team in the division with a negative differential.</p><p>Fudging the numbers sure helps, though. If you take away (get it?) the Bears’ 12 turnovers in their three worst games — five against the Bucs, five against the Packers and two against the Vikings — they’re averaging less than one per outing and are a perfectly wonderful plus-five. See how easy that was?</p><p><b>3. Good, better, give it a rest? </b>Not to tell coach Ben Johnson how to do his job, but he might want to get a new post-win chant warming up in the bullpen. If you watched the video the Bears put out of the locker-room scene Sunday, you might agree the “Good, better, best!” sounded anticlimactic and fell flat. Is a Super Bowl contender going to keep on chanting the same thing, <i>ad infinitum</i>, even after its ugliest of victories? Eventually, there will be a pair of water skis and an Arthur Fonzarelli leather jacket with Johnson’s name on them.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">"Our best football is yet to come" <a href="https://t.co/c3XpbnREtS">pic.twitter.com/c3XpbnREtS</a></p>— Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) <a href="https://x.com/ChicagoBears/status/2119666739889725791?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 9, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Caleb-o-meter: 4 out of 10</b></h3><p>In one impossibly bad quarter, Williams went overboard in paying tribute to Jay Cutler, who rarely was far removed from his last egregious pick thrown while backpedaling.</p><p>Wizardry in the face of pressure, it was not.</p><p>“I’m typically the big eraser,” Williams said.</p><p>If only there were an eraser big enough to wipe this performance from our memories.</p><h3><b>Not halfway bad</b></h3><p><b>The NFL’s top five teams at midseason:</b> 1. Bills, 2. 49ers, 3. Jaguars, 4. Bears, 5. Broncos.</p><p><b>Top five players, offense:</b> 1. Josh Allen, QB, Bills; 2. Joe Burrow, QB, Bengals; 3. Kenneth Walker III, RB, Chiefs; 4. Jordan Love, QB, Packers; 5. Jaxon Smith-Njigba, WR, Seahawks.</p><p><b>Top five players, defense:</b> 1. Will Anderson Jr., DE, Texans; 2. Fred Warner, LB, 49ers; 3. Jeffery Simmons, DT, Bears; 4. Greg Rousseau, LB, Bills; 5. Chase Young, DE, Saints.</p><p><b>Top five coaches: </b>1. John Harbaugh, Giants; 2. Johnson, Bears; 3. Kyle Shanahan, 49ers; 4. Liam Coen, Jaguars; 5. Sean Payton, Broncos.</p><p>You're free to quibble with my selections. I shall allow it this one time only.</p><h3><b>Department of redundancy department</b></h3><p>Even after the Vikings’ 23-6 loss to the Bills — only the sick and twisted could’ve watched such a display until the end — the NFC North is 20-4 against opponents from outside the division. At 7-0, the Bears lead the way.</p><p>The only other divisions checking in with winning records against the rest of the league are the AFC North at 16-8 and the NFC West at 14-9.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/09/bears-buccaneers-qb-baker-mayfield-accuse-mimicking-snap-count-cadence" target="_blank" >Bucs QB Baker Mayfield accuses Bears of mimicking his cadence</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/09/bears-qb-caleb-williams-must-use-4-interception-game-vs-buccaneers-to-to-keep-growing" >Bears QB Caleb Williams must use four-interception game vs. Buccaneers to keep growing</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/08/bears-grades-buccaneers-caleb-williams-ben-johnson-chicago-sunday-night-soldier-field-nfl" >Bears’ grades are in. How did they do against the Buccaneers?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Los votantes de Chicago apoyan abrumadoramente un recinto dedicado para festivales de música
entries.summary: <p>Los habitantes de Chicago quieren que la Ciudad desarrolle un espacio permanente para festivales de música a gran escala y eventos al aire libre.</p><p>Ese fue el mensaje en las urnas la semana pasada, cuando el 68% de los votantes apoyó la medida no vinculante en la boleta introducida por la concejal Nicole Lee (11.º).</p><p>“Honestamente, no estaba segura de cómo iba a salir eso”, dijo Lee el día después de que llegaron los resultados. “Mientras miraba los conteos, pensé: ‘Oh, esto va bastante bien’”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e80000" name="module-e80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La medida, destinada a medir el interés público, llegó después de las protestas en los últimos años de algunos residentes de Chicago que se oponen a que festivales gestionados por entidades privadas se celebren en espacios públicos de la ciudad, desde Lollapalooza en Grant Park hasta Riot Fest en Douglass Park.</p><p>Pero a pesar del apoyo electoral, no hay pasos claros a seguir. Por su parte, Lee — cuyo distrito incluye partes de Bridgeport y Chinatown, donde hay al menos una propuesta para una ubicación alternativa para un estadio de los Bears— dijo que le gustaría mantener viva la conversación.</p><p>“No tenía grandes expectativas sobre lo que vendría de inmediato”, dijo Lee. “Creo que después del COVID, y con el Centro que sigue teniendo dificultades para recuperarse, debemos pensar en crear y repartir un poco más la riqueza, crear centros económicos”.</p><p>En comparación con los espacios verdes públicos como Grant Park o Douglass Park, que actualmente albergan grandes festivales, Lee dijo que piensa que un destino con mejor infraestructura, incluidos baños permanentes, podría servir mejor a los asistentes y prevenir daños a los parques de la ciudad.</p><p>Tanto Lollapalooza como Riot Fest cayeron en fines de semana empapados por la lluvia este año, lo que dejó los parques anfitriones destrozados y enlodados. Los organizadores de festivales están contractualmente obligados a pagar por la reparación de los campos, pero los vecinos alrededor de Douglass Park, por ejemplo, se han quejado de que las reparaciones avanzan lentamente y dejan secciones del terreno inutilizables para el público durante largos periodos.</p><p>Las condiciones de lodo y la falta de infraestructura de accesibilidad también generan preocupaciones entre los asistentes con discapacidades.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/nNCaC2lrcRA?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Douglass Park the morning after Riot Fest versus one month later"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Algunos simpatizantes han comparado la idea propuesta con el recinto de Summerfest en Milwaukee, que es propiedad de esa Ciudad. El lugar opera todo el año a través de una organización sin fines de lucro. Pero al proponer la medida, Lee dijo que también tenía en mente a la organización sin fines de lucro de North Shore, Ravinia.</p><p>“La pregunta para mí era, ¿cómo sería la experiencia?”, dijo Lee. “Me encanta ir a Ravinia y tener una estructura permanente y esa predictibilidad. Seguimos hablando de predictibilidad y estabilidad, y para mí eso se siente como algo que se puede hacer de esa manera”.</p><p>Incluso si la idea mantiene impulso, también está la cuestión de dónde podrían ubicarse posibles terrenos para festivales.</p><p>“Tenemos muchos vecindarios distintos que tienen terrenos disponibles”, dijo Lee.</p><p>¿Podría Soldier Field ser una opción si los Chicago Bears se mudan del estadio frente al lago?</p><p>“Creo que Soldier Field es una oportunidad para eso”, dijo Lee al Sun-Times antes del día de las elecciones. “Si los Bears se mudan, tenemos que encontrarle otro propósito. Sabemos que el uso del recinto para conciertos y otro tipo de eventos es lucrativo para la Ciudad y el distrito de parques al final del día, así que creo que nos conviene realmente buscar esas oportunidades”.</p><p>La organizadora comunitaria, Sara Heymann, del grupo Únete La Villita, que lleva años impulsando que Riot Fest salga de Douglass Park, señaló el nuevo desarrollo del South Loop conocido como The 78 o el sitio de los antiguos Damen Silos como lugares posibles para un espacio para eventos al aire libre. No importa dónde esté, Heymann quiere que esté cerca del transporte público y completamente accesible.</p><p>Chicago ya posee varios recintos al aire libre, como el pabellón operado por la Ciudad en Millennium Park. Sin embargo, ese recinto diseñado por Frank Gehry suele usarse para festivales de acceso gratuito, como Blues Fest y Jazz Fest.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-aaf12b" name="image-aaf12b"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f5db661/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4610x2587+0+242/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F45%2F30%2F699ef67b47cba1f0832101d35132%2Fnortherlyisland-260911-06.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1ed8976/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4610x2587+0+242/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F45%2F30%2F699ef67b47cba1f0832101d35132%2Fnortherlyisland-260911-06.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3ad7bf6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4610x2587+0+242/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F45%2F30%2F699ef67b47cba1f0832101d35132%2Fnortherlyisland-260911-06.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Algunos señalan el recinto en Northerly Island, propiedad de la Ciudad y operado por Live Nation, como una advertencia sobre cómo podría ser un terreno permanente para festivales. Los críticos aseguran que ese modelo deja fuera a artistas y eventos independientes." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3ad7bf6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4610x2587+0+242/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F45%2F30%2F699ef67b47cba1f0832101d35132%2Fnortherlyisland-260911-06.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/326495a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4610x2587+0+242/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F45%2F30%2F699ef67b47cba1f0832101d35132%2Fnortherlyisland-260911-06.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3ad7bf6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4610x2587+0+242/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F45%2F30%2F699ef67b47cba1f0832101d35132%2Fnortherlyisland-260911-06.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Algunos señalan el recinto en Northerly Island, propiedad de la Ciudad y operado por Live Nation, como una advertencia sobre cómo podría ser un terreno permanente para festivales. Los críticos aseguran que ese modelo deja fuera a artistas y eventos independientes.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>En otros lugares, la Ciudad también es dueña de Northerly Island, pero contrata la operación del Huntington Bank Pavilion en ese sitio a Live Nation. Ese arreglo está bajo escrutinio en un nuevo informe de la Universidad de Vanderbilt, que halló que esos acuerdos son desproporcionadamente favorables a Live Nation al renunciar a licitaciones competitivas, ofrecer rentas por debajo del mercado y darle a la corporación la posibilidad de vender los derechos de nombre de los recintos de propiedad pública.</p><p>Tras la circulación de la medida en la boleta, algunos expresaron preocupación por lo que un lugar así podría significar para los recintos más pequeños e independientes de la ciudad, muchos de los cuales han tenido dificultades económicas en los últimos años. En un video en redes sociales, el equipo detrás de Bookclub Chicago señaló al recinto gestionado por Live Nation en Northerly Island como advertencia.</p><p>Lee está abierta a considerar la idea de un recinto gestionado y operado por la Ciudad.</p><p>“Creo que eso puede generar ingresos”, dijo el miércoles, pero agregó, “Creo que si podemos ser creativos con un socio, creo que hay posibilidades que valen la pena explorar”.</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers es reportera de artes y cultura en WBEZ. </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Bears work out DT Jordan Elliott
entries.summary: <p>Defensive tackle Jordan Elliott was one of the players the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> worked out Tuesday, according to ESPN. Elliott was released by the Titans last month after an incident at the team’s facility.</p><p>That does not necessarily mean a signing is imminent. Teams often work out players to keep their scouting reports updated in case of future needs.</p><p>Last month, Elliott got in an argument with Titans right tackle JC Latham and went to his car to get a gun before the incident was de-escalated. Titans coach Robert Saleh said then that “rules are rules with regard to guns” on team property. He was not arrested.</p><p>“He’s a good man … ” Saleh said. “Had a terrible lapse in judgment that I recognize as a call for help more than a criminal act. He’s never committed a crime in his entire life and he pulled a gun in the parking lot.”</p><p>Elliott played for Saleh with the 49ers. The Titans signed him a two-year, $8 million deal during the offseason. He’s familiar with Jeffery Simmons, the former Titans star for whom the Bears traded late last month.</p><p>Elliott has started 65 games in seven seasons with the Browns, 49ers and Titans. He’s considered a solid run defender.</p><p>The Bears don’t have a glaring need at the position, even after losing Kentavius Street for the season because of a knee injury last week. Simmons played 97% of the Bears’ defensive snaps Sunday night, while fellow defensive tackle Grady Jarrett played 76% of the time.</p>

entries.title: How Janelle James went from Champaign stand-up to ‘Abbott Elementary’ to Netflix
entries.summary: <p>When Netflix approached Janelle James about recording an hourlong comedy special, she knew she had to tape it in Chicago, specifically at the Vic Theatre in Lake View.</p><p>“I didn't even contemplate doing any other places,” said James, who is best known for her role as principal Ava Coleman in the Emmy-winning ABC sitcom “Abbott Elementary.”</p><p>“I love Chicago,” said James, who got her start in comedy and stand-up in the Midwest, while living in Champaign, Illinois. “It's always been one of my favorite places to perform. Chicago just seems more open and out. It was very important to me to get a good cross-section of people, some of everything in the audience.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/MeBysXIz-zM?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Janelle James: How Romantic | Sneak Peek | Netflix"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Her Netflix comedy special “How Romantic” debuts Tuesday . The routine is James’ first hourlong comedy special to hit the streaming platform after giving shorter sets in Netflix’s 2018 “The Comedy Lineup” and later, on Season 3 of the network’s “The Standups.”</p><p>Though “How Romantic” begins with a humorous acknowledgment of today’s political landscape, James said her comedy has “lightened up” a bit since her first two Netflix specials.</p><p>“I've always been like this, unfortunately,” she told this reporter, laughing, on a video interview call a few days before the special aired. “Always reading the news and depressing myself.” </p><p>From a young age, her father called her “The Daily News” since she always knew the neighborhood gossip. As a young girl, she’d retell those stories in her own comedic way.</p><p>“That's part of the challenge of being a comedian, is making awful things funny in some ways,” said James, 47. “I wanted people to know that I am, especially for this special, appearing as myself. I am not there as the character.”</p><p>Over the approximately hourlong special, James talks about her experiences with men in relationships and dating, her love of dark humor and life in Los Angeles. Later bits of the comedy special detail James’ refusal to pay for an ambulance despite now being “wealth adjacent” and why she thinks men and women should engage in a “little light tusslin.”</p><div I wouldn't switch with any other character on the show,” she continued. “As the seasons go on, you can see why she is the way she is.”</p><p>James was born in the U.S. Virgin Islands, and she began working on her dad’s food truck as a 9-year-old. The actor said her childhood makes her relate to Ava’s humanity and “hustler mentality,” especially as the oldest of nine siblings, James moved to New York at 16.</p><p>But she ended up in Champaign after her then-husband landed a teaching job in the Midwest.</p><p>“I probably would have never started comedy if I was never there,” she said.</p><p>It all happened by chance: Someone handed James a flyer for an open mic as she did some grocery shopping one day. She decided to show up.</p><p>“It was at a biker bar called Memphis On Main,” she said, noting that Champaign’s main corridor is no more than a few blocks. There, she learned the importance of practicing and rehearsing your material.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Playing Ava on “Abbott Elementary” has helped her realize “You can be and look like this and still be respected and still have opinions and still be a boss b - - - -.”</p><p>She never imagined herself in a role like the one she scored on ABC, but the comedian-actor said: “I feel like everything I do is kismet. entries.title: Cops question person of interest after home invasion, sexual assault at gunpoint in Auburn Gresham
entries.summary: <p>Area 2 detectives are interviewing a person of interest Tuesday after someone burst into a 19-year-old woman's home, sexually assaulted her at gunpoint and robbed her last week in Auburn Gresham. </p><p>No charges have been announced in the attack, which occurred Friday about 10:30 a.m. in the 7700 block of South <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/09/gunman-bursts-into-gresham-home-sexually-assaults-woman-police-say" target="_blank" >Racine Avenue, according to police.</a> The woman was home alone when a man — believed to be 40 to 55 years old — forced his way inside, armed with a handgun and sexually assaulted her, police said.</p><p>The woman <a class="Link" href="https://abc7chicago.com/post/auburn-gresham-chicago-crime-person-interest-custody-home-invasion-sex-assault/20030262/" target="_blank" >told ABC7 that she waited more than four hours</a> for police to arrive after she called 911 multiple times.</p><p>Cook County Crime Stoppers is offering a $1,000 reward for any information that leads to an arrest in the case.</p><p>Area 2 detectives are investigating. </p>

entries.title: Rep. Nikki Budzinski elected chair of moderate New Dem Coalition, vows Dems will lower costs for Americans
entries.summary: <p>U.S. Rep. Nikki Budzinski, a Peoria Democrat and former aide to both Gov. JB Pritzker and President Joe Biden, was elected on Tuesday to serve as chair of the center-left group known as the New Democrat Coalition. </p><p>Elected to the 13th Congressional District seat in 2022, Budzinski served as executive director of Pritzker's transition team after his 2018 election and later served as a senior adviser once he took office. She also served as chief of staff in President Biden's Office of Management and Budget for about six months before running for office. She previously worked as Hillary Clinton's labor outreach director in 2016 for her presidential campaign. </p><p>In a speech before the chair election, Budzinski warned that despite decisive wins, the stakes are high for Democrats to earn voters' trust and deliver results within the next two years.</p><p>"They want us to provide relief to the crushing cost of living and root out corruption. Based on these two priorities, the American people voted for massive change on November 3rd. The New Dems will deliver on this mandate in the 120th Congress by getting common-sense legislation to the President’s desk," Budzinski said in her speech. "We have to be clear-eyed about the election results. Voters are not in love with us, but rather giving Democrats an opportunity to show them that we can deliver. If we fail at this mission, voters could return us to the realities of either small majorities or worse, the minority again. The stakes are high."</p><p>Budzinski spoke in support of Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries becoming the country's first Black House speaker. And she outlined some of her top priorities for the caucus, including holding the Trump administration accountable for "reckless tariff policies," ending the war in Iran, passing paid family medical leave and raising the minimum wage. She also spoke in support of improving housing policy and making the country's health care system "affordable and accessible for all." </p><p>The New Democrat Coalition has 40 new members, swelling to 142 members and members-elect in the 120th Congress, and the group says its goal is to lower costs and fight corruption. The Congressional Progressive Caucus on Sunday said it now has 105 members, including six progressive candidates who won red districts. </p><p>Democrats were emboldened by nationwide wins that reshaped American politics and offered a sharp rejection of some of President Donald Trump's top policies. The blue wave may actually spark some cooperation within the U.S. House, with the Congressional Progressive Caucus and the New Democrat Coalition both wanting to help Americans who are struggling to make ends meet.</p><p>Budzinski, a moderate, defeated Republican candidate Jeff Wilson 64.9% to 35.1% last week. Budzinski's district encompasses central Illinois cities like Decatur, Springfield and Urbana and stretches south all the way to Belleville. </p><p>U.S. Rep. Brad Schneider, D-Illinois, previously served as chair of the coalition. </p><p>"New Dems have grown from slightly more than 40 Members when I was first elected 14 years ago to the 142-Member powerhouse it is today,” Schneider said in a statement. “Amidst the chaos of this Republican majority, New Dems have remained focused on the practical solutions the American people are demanding and getting ready for this moment."</p>

entries.title: Why Spencer Knight is perturbed by Blackhawks demoting Arvid Soderblom: 'Just isn't right'
entries.summary: <p>It isn't sitting right with Spencer Knight that his former goalie partner, Arvid Soderblom, was the only player sent down to Rockford after the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' disastrous road trip.</p><p>"Sody, to be real, has only played like four games," Knight said Tuesday. "I feel like giving up someone like that who had only played that many games, [and had] been put in tough situations, to me just isn't right."</p><p>The Hawks' coaching staff has indeed leaned heavily on Knight so far this season, starting him 14 times in 18 games — including in all nine home games. Soderblom's four starts had all come on the road, including a matinee and the second half of a back-to-back.</p><p>Reading between the lines, it sounds like Knight doesn't believe Soderblom got enough playing time to be justly blamed for the team's 4-13-1 record.</p><p>"I'm sure he wanted, [at] times, to play better," Knight said. "There's a lot of times where everyone wants to play better. But if [sending down] 'Sody' is the only thing we do, I'd rather them come to me and put something on me, blame me or something. I've played most of the games.</p><p>"I'd rather take the heat than have him take the heat if that's the only thing we do. No one has talked to me about it, and frankly I think I deserve more of the blame."</p><p>Knight's viewpoint is understandable, but Soderblom's lengthy track record as a statistically subpar NHL goalie — combined with his especially acute struggles in his aforementioned four starts this season — did seem to justify a change.</p><p>Nevertheless, it's very fair to question why Soderblom's demotion is the only change the Hawks have yet made to their entire roster. Nobody else has been waived or traded, even though general manager Kyle Davidson — who's scheduled to hold a news conference Wednesday — has reportedly been exploring trade options.</p><p>Knight mentioned how the team "talks about accountability and what we want to hold the standard to be." And there's no doubt Soderblom isn't the only Hawk whose performance to date hasn't met those standards.</p><p>After all, Soderblom isn't responsible whatsoever for the fact the Hawks have allowed the most two-on-one rushes in the league, or that they've surely had among the most failed defensive-zone exits, too.</p><p>The Hawks hope <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/09/blackhawks-systems-changes-jeff-blashill-wyatt-kaiser-defense" >hammering down</a> on some system tweaks and points of emphasis in practices this week will help, but the lack of bigger changes is certainly curious.</p><p>It's also curious that the Hawks haven't yet committed to Drew Commesso — who was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/08/blackhawks-backup-goalie-change-arvid-soderblom-waivers" >called up</a> Sunday to replace Soderblom — sticking in the NHL moving forward.</p><p>Coach Jeff Blashill said the team determined they "needed a little bit more" from the backup goalie role, but he has given several evasive answers when asked specifically about Commesso.</p><p>"Right now, he’s here, and Spencer is our starter and he’s the backup," Blashill said Tuesday. "We wouldn’t have recalled him if that wasn’t the case. But I also don’t want to get too far ahead of myself on anything. That’s not fair to anyone involved."</p><p>As for Knight, his numbers — including his .881 save percentage and negative-3.7 GSAA — are down from last season. For comparison, Soderblom had an .842 save percentage and negative-6.4 GSAA.</p><p>The Hawks' defense has made life difficult for Knight, however, even if he hasn't stolen as many wins for them as he did early last season. He has faced the second-most high-danger shots per minute among all goalies leaguewide.</p><p>"There's always frustration," Knight said. "But I try to channel that frustration more toward, 'I should've done this. I should've done that.' Not being like, 'What's going on in front of me?'</p><p>"At the end of the day, that's all I can control. Once you start trying to control the externals, you find yourself not enjoying and not focusing on your process."</p>

entries.title: Bulls preparing for French connection as Wemby and Spurs come to town
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> don’t have an Eiffel Tower.</p><p>There’s only one of those in the NBA right now and Victor Wembanyama will be on full display Wednesday night when the Spurs come to the United Center.</p><p>No, the draft lottery only smiled on San Antonio that 2023 season, importing the French phenom to U.S. soil.</p><p>The hope the Bulls do hold onto? Maybe, just maybe, they have to settle for the Mont Saint-Michel. Not nearly as majestic, nowhere as iconic, and very few postcards being sent out, but one of the more resilient natural defensive fortresses in all of France.</p><p>That’s the vision they have for Noa Essengue, and the outlook the second-year player suddenly has for himself.</p><p>“My teammates and coach, the whole organization, trusts me to guard the best player,” Essengue said on Tuesday. “I talked to (coach) Tiago (Splitter), with (former Bulls coach) Billy (Donovan) last year, and Tiago told me if you do that one thing right, you’re going to get more and more (playing time).”</p><p>A message that didn’t initially hit home without some tough love.</p><p>When Splitter was hired from Portland in the offseason, he didn’t know what he had in the French kid who was selected No. 12 overall as an admitted project and spent all but six minutes of last season in street clothes because of season-ending shoulder surgery.</p><p>Then when he did coach him in Summer League, he had even more concerns. No energy, no physicality, too emotional. Splitter actually benched Essengue in Game 1 and made him a reserve. A move that put the ball in Essengue’s court.</p><p>After all, the front office and coaching staff were all new. They had no allegiance to Essengue’s development. It was sink or swim for the 19-year-old. He chose the latter.</p><p>“It shows he’s a winner, he’s a resilient player,” Splitter said. “He wants to do the right thing. He wants to do what the coaching staff feels is the right thing to do for him. When we got back from (Summer League) he came to me and asked, ‘What should I do?’ I said you’ve got to defend, make good decisions on offense and crash the boards, and that’s exactly what he’s doing. So I’m glad he’s coachable, he’s working on it. It’s not easy to play defense. It’s a tough job. People don’t talk too much in the media when you’re a good defender, and he’s just going for it. Doing the little things that matter to be honest.”</p><p>Still with some hiccups but getting better.</p><p>Essengue’s role is simple coming off the bench: Pickup the best opposing player full-court and make his life difficult. He still fouls too much, he still lacks physicality at times, but it’s a work in progress.</p><p>“Just get more physical, that’s the main point,” Essengue said of the next step. “Guys are trying to bully me and things like that so get low to the ground and be more physical.”</p><p>As for the other French guy that will be in the gym Wednesday night, well, for a Bulls team that has one of the least efficient offenses so far this season, good luck.</p><p>“We talk about this every time we play against him,” Splitter added of Wembanyama. “What people don’t say as much is he changes the game the most on defense because you don’t have easy shots against him, right. Even getting close to the rim is hard because of his (7-foot-4) size. We have to be very mindful of when to attack the rim, how to attack the rim, do it and be prepared for it.”</p>

entries.title: Amazon drone delivery center in Markham set for takeoff
entries.summary: <p>Amazon cut the ribbon on its new drone delivery center in Markham Tuesday afternoon.</p><p>Drone deliveries are set to begin "this fall" from the new center at 2201 W. 159th St., according to the company. </p><p>In August, Amazon <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/amazon-drone-delivery-expansion-walmart-20db399ba65e8bc36a76b547f990b118" target="_blank" >announced</a> it was expanding its airborne shipping to suburban areas in nearly 500 U.S. cities, including the Chicago, Atlanta, Cleveland and Boise, Idaho, metro areas. The drones will primarily fly in the suburbs, away from skyscrapers and major airports that could cause problems, with each drone site serving multiple cities.</p><p>The drones can carry only packages weighing up to five pounds, and they face countless challenges — concerns about noise, interference from tree cover and landscaping, and pools, which can make it hard to find a drop-off zone.</p><p>Walmart already offers drone delivery at more than 75 stores across Arkansas, Florida, North Carolina, Georgia and Texas, though the retailer mainly relies on drivers for deliveries. Walmart earlier this year said it planned to expand <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/drones-delivery-orders-available-walmart-amazon-e1dbd3638c60e464d6533e74eb046ce6" target="_blank" >drone delivery service</a> to 150 more stores in partnership with Wing, a division of Google parent company Alphabet, giving it 270 drone delivery locations by 2027.</p><p><i>Contributing: entries.title: ‘Heartbreaking and entirely preventable’: Chicago-area man died after deportation, family attorney says
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago area-man who had no criminal record and suffered from multiple chronic health conditions died shortly after a deportation flight to Pakistan, his lawyer said Tuesday.</p><p>Sixty-one-year-old Ayaz Ahmed of Morton Grove was arrested in June by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and faced deportation for having an expired visa, said his attorney Hashim Siddique. Siddique said Ahmed’s family hired him to expedite his deportation because they feared his health would deteriorate in custody.</p><p>Ahmed needed a breathing device, nasal spray and medication for chronic conditions, according to Siddique, who also mentioned high blood pressure and a possible heart condition.</p><p>Prior to the July flight to Pakistan, Ahmed had been detained at the Clay County Detention center in Indiana, according to Siddique.</p><p>Around June 10, Siddique contacted the detention center after Ahmed’s family raised concerns about whether he was receiving prescribed medication. A jail officer, Siddique shared, assured him Ahmed was receiving them.</p><p>Siddique also spoke directly with Ahmed, who told him he was getting the medication at that time but he could not confirm whether this was being done consistently.</p><p>“He may have been [receiving his medication] when I spoke to him, but I don’t know if he was receiving it daily,” he said. “That I don't know.”</p><p>He said he notified ICE of Ahmed’s medical needs and was told those concerns would be forwarded to the detention center.</p><p>Siddique said Clay County officials repeatedly told him that detainees could request medical care through electronic tablets. But Ahmed was not fluent in English and Siddique questioned whether he was able to properly use the system.</p><p>On June 18, Siddique learned Ahmed had been placed in medical isolation. He said a Clay County officer cited claustrophobia but the circumstances surrounding the isolation remain unclear. He described medical isolation as similar to solitary confinement, with Ahmed alone in a cell.</p><p>Clay County officials confirmed Ahmed was in detention there but would not answer questions about his medical care.</p><p>In the days before his deportation, Ahmed was transferred through several detention facilities, according to Siddique. On July 24 Ahmed was moved to Jackson Parrish Correctional Center in Louisiana; three days later, he was transferred to Camp East Montana in El Paso, Texas, and on July 29 to Prairieland Detention Center in Alvarado, Texas.</p><p>Siddique said he does not know whether Ahmed received his prescribed medication at each facility or during the deportation flight.</p><p>“He keeps getting transferred, and then I'm not sure if everything went with him, “Siddique said.</p><p>Alexa Van Brunt, director of the Illinois office of the MacArthur Justice Center, is part of a legal team that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/10/29/civil-rights-aclu-lawsuit-indiana-immigration-detention-center" >recently filed a class-action lawsuit </a>challenging conditions at Miami Correctional Facility, an Indiana prison that also holds ICE detainees. The lawsuit alleges inadequate medical care, delays in receiving prescribed medications, prolonged solitary confinement and unsanitary conditions.</p><p>Van Brunt said frequent transfers between detention facilities pose another risk for people with chronic illnesses.</p><p>“That’s another impediment to proper care because there’s no continuity of care for people with chronic diseases like cancer or diabetes,” she said.</p><p>Siddique said he tracked Ahmed’s transfers between detention facilities through ICE notifications but received no flight itinerary or updates during the journey.</p><p>ICE officials said Ahmed was medically cleared for travel and was no longer in their custody when he died.</p><p>“No medical emergencies occurred during the flight, no signs of medical distress were observed, and no individuals required hospitalization upon landing,” the agency said in a statement.</p><p>ICE said Ahmed received all his scheduled medication during the flight.</p><p>“Any claims of neglect or mistreatment are categorically FALSE,” the agency said.</p><p>But after the plane landed, Ahmed allegedly collapsed on the tarmac in Pakistan.</p><p>Siddique said Ahmed’s son emailed him saying his father died seven hours after landing in Islamabad.</p><p>ICE officials said once Ahmed was transferred to the custody of the Pakistani government, they no longer had “authority over their care or access to their medical or official records.”</p><p>Ahmed’s family is exploring legal action, according to Siddique.</p><p>Some Chicago advocates are calling for an independent criminal investigation into Ahmed’s death and ICE’s medical standards.</p><p>“This heartbreaking and entirely preventable tragedy lays bare the harrowing human cost of rushed, aggressive immigration enforcement,” Ahmed Rehab, executive director of CAIR-Chicago, said in a statement.</p><p>The Pakistan Consulate in Chicago and the Pakistani Embassy did not respond to requests for comment.</p>

entries.title: School mourns death of Evanston high school senior in Deerfield crash
entries.summary: <p>A suburban community is mourning after an Evanston Township high school student was killed in a crash early Monday.</p><p>Charles Halliday, 17, was driving an Audi SUV when he crashed with a box truck just after midnight Monday in the 1100 block of Waukegan Road in Deerfield, according to the Lake County Coroner’s Office.</p><p>Halliday, of Evanston, was pronounced dead at the scene, according to the Deerfield Police Department. The coroner’s office said Halliday died from blunt force trauma.</p><p>Halliday was a senior and member of the theater community at Evanston Township High School.</p><p>“The time, talent and care he gave to this community were meaningful to so many, and his presence made a difference in ways that will always be remembered,” Principal Quiana McNeal said. “His loss will be deeply felt by the many students, staff members, and others whose lives he touched.”</p><p>McNeal encouraged students who needed support to reach out to an adult for help.</p><p>“Our hearts are with Charles's family, friends, teachers, and all who knew and loved him,” McNeal said. “As a school community, we will hold space for one another and support those who are grieving in the days ahead.”</p>

entries.title: Bears stick with roster as is at trade deadline; Vikings bring back QB Kirk Cousins
entries.summary: <p>The trade deadline was quiet for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> on Tuesday since they already made their big move by trading two first-round picks for star defensive tackle <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/03/el-jefe-takes-charge-dt-jeffery-simmons-embraces-role-responsibility-as-new-boss-of-bears-defense" target="_blank" >Jeffery Simmons</a> two weeks ago. That’ll probably be the answer this time next year, too, given how much draft capital they spent on that deal.</p><p>That’s as all in as a team can realistically go.</p><p>They made no moves at the deadline and had every reason to believe they can keep winning with the roster they already have. Coach Ben Johnson said Monday he was “really confident” with his team as it was, and it’s hard to argue with him when the Bears stand atop the NFC North at 7-2.</p><p>The Bears, who are on their bye week, also moved into the No. 2 seed in the NFC, a hair behind the 49ers at 7-1.</p><p>They pulled into first place in the division because the Vikings got blown out at home by the Bills on Monday night and slipped into a tie for second with the Lions at 6-2. The Packers are right behind them at 6-3 in the NFL’s toughest and tightest division.</p><p>That loss could be the start of a slide for the Vikings, and they tried to stop it Tuesday by trading a third-round pick to the Raiders to bring back longtime quarterback Kirk Cousins. He was their starter from 2018 through ’23 before they tried to start over with first-round pick J.J. McCarthy.</p><p>In between, they had Sam Darnold and let him walk in free agency. He won the Super Bowl with the Seahawks last season. Regrets abound in Minnesota.</p><p>Cousins, from Barrington, has played decently this season and could take the starting job from Kyler Murray. He certainly will start Sunday at the Packers in a game the Bears will watch closely.</p><p>Murray has been out with a hamstring injury, and the Vikings played Carson Wentz in his place against the Bills. Wentz completed 8 of 25 passes and threw two interceptions to finish with an 8.9 passer rating before getting benched in favor of Max Brosmer.</p><p>Considering their options, the Vikings were smart to pounce on Cousins. The Bears don’t play the Vikings again until the final game of the regular season, so there’s no telling who will be starting at quarterback for them at that point, but Cousins gives them a chance to stay in the race.</p><p>The Packers and Lions stood pat, too. The Packers might’ve been a good fit for Colts running back Jonathan Taylor, but they’re in a similar position as the Bears after trading two first-rounders for Micah Parsons last year.</p><p>The Lions’ only move Tuesday was trading a 2028 sixth-round pick to the Jets for safety Andre Cisco. They swept the Bears last season and seem content to go after them as constructed.</p><p>The Bears certainly have needs even after trading for Simmons and could’ve added help at cornerback, defensive end and maybe even on the offensive line, but they would’ve been shopping the bargain aisle. They have five picks in the 2027 draft: a second, third, fifth, sixth and seventh. That’s not much ammunition.</p><p>The top realistic targets were Chargers pass rusher Khalil Mack, Jets cornerback Nahshon Wright and Eagles cornerback Riq Woolen. It would’ve been a splashy move for Bears general manager Ryan Poles to bring back Mack, whom he traded to the Chargers in 2022 after Mack made three Pro Bowls for the Bears.</p><p>At 35, Mack might have been available for a fifth-rounder, but he said he didn’t wish to be traded, and the winless Chargers opted against a fire sale.</p><p>Wright, who made the Pro Bowl for the Bears last season, might still be an option. He left in free agency for a one-year, $3.5 million contract, but hasn’t played a snap defensively for the Jets this season. He has played three games, appearing only on special teams.</p><p>The Bears had a relatively dim outlook on Wright after a season in which he had five interceptions and two forced fumbles but wasn’t consistently reliable in coverage. It seemed unlikely he would beat out Tyrique Stevenson or anyone they drafted — they took Malik Muhammad in the fourth round — for a starting job, and that’s still true, but he could be a helpful depth piece if the Jets release him.</p><p>Other than trading for Simmons, the Bears have been counting on help from within. Their roster improved when nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon returned, they should have No. 2 running back Kyle Monangai back when they resume Nov. 22 against the Saints and they’re hopeful safety Coby Bryant could come off injured reserve next month.</p><p>They’re bullish on the players already in their building, and they've earned the right to be.</p>
